cells.tense: Here, you point your attention at one thing and mean it, without bracing.
cells.act: hold your shape under the weight
cells.ask: Take whatever you're carrying this week and keep it at the weight it actually has — don't trim it for anyone, don't inflate it either. Steady, as it is.
cells.core:
You can pick a direction right now, and the picking arrives out of clarity rather than out of something behind you pushing. Saying this, not that, and meaning it. The shape of it going well is a direction you chose, held without forcing, the ground staying steady while you hold it.

There's weight somewhere. The pull is to grip it tighter, or shove it aside before it's had time. Carry it as it is instead. Don't make it smaller so someone relaxes, don't make it larger so it seems urgent. Keep it for the week at the weight it came with. Carrying it isn't deciding anything — that's the point — and you'll still be standing at the end, and nothing will have swollen.

cells.tense: Bracing now, you'll steer a clearing that hasn't finished happening yet.
cells.act: look at the same thing longer, until it shows you more
cells.ask: Give one situation you've been forcing forward two more weeks of looking — same eyes, just longer — and let what wasn't there the first time show up.
cells.core:
A structure comes down fast, and the impulse is to raise the next one faster, before the dust has settled. You'll steer the clearing while it's still going, push outcomes to land before they're due, white-knuckle reality just to keep it in one shape. It will feel like direction. From outside it can look like someone running to catch a thing that wasn't falling.

Seeing a pattern and closing it aren't the same move. Look at what you've got a while longer — don't rule on it, don't repair it, just keep your eyes on it. Recognition that goes on deepening shows more than a quick verdict does. What's true about this is already sitting there. It needs more looking, not more steering.

cells.tense: You've stood at a closed door long past knocking, waiting for it to reopen.
cells.act: do one thing today the way only you do it, and do not explain it
cells.ask: Today, do one task the way you actually do it — how you walk somewhere, how you answer a message. No explaining it to anyone after.
cells.core:
The direction that belongs to you is still in you, but it's been quiet. Something that came down left open ground, and some days it's easier to stand there than to pick a way to face. Not because you can't. Because the last turning meant something, and part of you is still back at it, waiting.

What brings you forward isn't pushing harder. A flat battery doesn't charge because you demand it. So: today, one task done your way — not better, not more impressive, just yours. Nothing after it, no explanation, no follow-up. Doing it is what turns the current back on. Doing it your way is the whole act, not a step toward a bigger one.

cells.tense: Right now you're heading somewhere, and the story is that you're just following along.
cells.act: put your own name on what is already yours
cells.ask: Find something you've built or kept going and would shrug off as 'just what I do' — then once, on paper, set your name to it. Not for credit.
cells.core:
Direction moves through you here and mostly goes unnoticed. All day you're picking this and not that — it happens, it has shape, it goes somewhere — but the account you keep says nobody's steering, that you're riding momentum, that anyone in your spot would do the same.

What fell wasn't your life. Something false came down, and what's left is still yours. The turn doesn't need to be dramatic. Take something you've made or kept going, a thing with your fingerprints on it, and quietly set your name to it, on paper rather than announced. Not a trophy, not a performance. Just: this is mine, and it was chosen. Once is enough to see the hand was on the pen.

attempts.check: The draft's one unsupported claim would be any assertion about what the person's past actually held — Too Little must locate them behind a door already closed, never say what happened there or what it cost. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not stuck, I'm just tired,' and the ask still has to be useful: 'put your name on one thing you already made' does not require them to accept my read of their history, so it survives being wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about false structures 'collapsing' as though I know which of theirs is false — cut it. Ask verbs: 1 release/let finish, 2 look longer, 3 do one thing your way, 4 choose once deliberately — four different openings.
